gloss: cast up, heap up (a road, a mound); exalt
summary: To cast up: to heap earth and stones into a raised road and clear it of stones (Isa 57:14; 62:10), or into a mound against a city (Job 19:12; Jer 50:26); and, of a person, to raise high, as Wisdom who exalts the one who exalts her (Pro 4:8), or to set oneself up as a bank against Yahweh's people (Exo 9:17). Its nouns are the things cast up: the מְסִלָּה, a built-up highway, and above all the highway Yahweh's people are to prepare for him and on which the remnant return to Zion (Isa 11:16; 35:8; 40:3), which the Gospels apply to John preparing the way of Jesus; the סֹלְלָה, the siege mound poured out against a city; the סֻלָּם, the stairway of Jacob's dream. The psalms' סֶלָה and the basket סַל are kept here, but their tie to the root is not clear.

words.gloss: selah (a word set in the psalms; meaning not certain)
words.summary: Seventy-one times in thirty-nine psalms and three times in Habakkuk 3, a psalm with musical directions (Hab 3:1, 19). It stands outside the sentence, usually at the end of a verse or a stanza, sometimes mid-verse (Psa 55:20; 57:4; Hab 3:3, 9), and most of its psalms are headed “to the chief musician”. Scripture never explains it. Taking it from סָלַל as “lift up” (the voice, or the music) fits its place but rests on nothing in the text; the link to the root is not established, and no cognate bears on it.

senses.gloss: selah (a pause or direction in the psalms)
senses.definition: A word standing apart from the sentence at the close of a verse or section of a psalm, which the text does not explain; from its place and from the musical headings of its psalms, a direction for the singing or playing.

evidence.note: “Many say of my soul, There is no salvation for him in God. סֶלָה.” The first of three in the psalm, each closing a stanza (Psa 3:5, 9).
“Higgaion. סֶלָה”: set beside הִגָּיוֹן, the sounding of the lyre (Psa 92:4), as a word of the music.
“Upon the lyre with הִגָּיוֹן”: the meaning of the word set with סֶלָה in Psa 9:17.
“A prayer of Habakkuk the prophet, upon Shigionoth”: a psalm with musical directions.
Mid-verse: “The Holy One from Mount Paran. סֶלָה. His splendour covered the heavens.”
“To the chief musician, on my stringed instruments.”
Psa 46 closes each stanza with the same refrain and סֶלָה (Psa 46:8, 12).
Mid-verse, between “he who sits from of old” and the clause that follows.
Mid-verse.
“Kingdoms of the earth, sing to God, make music to the Lord. סֶלָה.”

words.summary: The road cast up (סָלַל, Isa 62:10): a made road, as against the fields and vineyards beside it (Num 20:19), running between towns (Jdg 21:19) or up to the gates (1Ch 26:16), on which one goes straight without turning aside (1Sa 6:12). The prophets make it the highway prepared for Yahweh and for the return of his people.

senses.definition: A made road between places, kept clear and travelled by people and armies, distinct from the open country beside it.

evidence.note: Israel to Edom: “By the highway (בַּמְסִלָּה) we will go up … only let me pass through on foot”; Num 20:17 adds, “we will not pass through field or vineyard … we will go by the king's way.”
Shiloh, “on the east of the highway that goes up from Bethel to Shechem”.
“On the highways, of which one goes up to Bethel and one to Gibeah.”
The cows went straight on the road to Beth-shemesh, “on one highway they went, lowing as they went, and turned not aside to the right or the left”.
Amasa lay wallowing in blood “in the middle of the highway”, and was moved “from the highway into the field”.
“By the conduit of the upper pool, which is on the highway of the Fuller's Field”; so Isa 7:3; 36:2.
“At the gate of Shallecheth, by the highway that goes up.”
“The highways are desolate, the wayfarer (עֹבֵר אֹרַח) ceases.”
“Set your heart toward the highway, the way (דֶּרֶךְ) you went; return, virgin of Israel.”
Of the wicked: “Wasting and destruction are in their highways; the way of peace they do not know” (Isa 59:8).
“The highway of the upright is to turn from evil; he who guards his way keeps his life.”

senses.gloss: the highway prepared for Yahweh and his people
senses.definition: In the prophets, the highway cast up through the desert for Yahweh's coming and for his scattered people's return to Zion; the Gospels apply it to John preparing the way for Jesus.

evidence.note: “In the wilderness clear the way of Yahweh; make straight in the desert a highway for our God.”
John is “he who was spoken of through Isaiah the prophet”: “make his paths (τρίβους) straight”.
John of himself: “I am the voice of one crying in the wilderness, Make straight the way of the Lord, as Isaiah the prophet said.”
“There will be a highway for the remnant of his people who remain from Assyria, as there was for Israel in the day he came up from the land of Egypt.”
“A highway from Egypt to Assyria.”
“I will make all my mountains a way, and my highways shall be raised up.”
“Cast up, cast up the highway (סֹלּוּ סֹלּוּ הַמְסִלָּה), clear it of stones”: the verb and its noun together.
“Blessed the man whose strength is in you, highways in their heart”: the pilgrims' roads up to Zion (Psa 84:8).

senses.definition: The way a thing keeps to as on a road: the course of the stars, the line of a marching soldier.

evidence.note: “From heaven they fought; the stars from their courses (מִמְּסִלּוֹתָם) fought against Sisera.”
Of the army of locusts: “Each walks in his highway (בִּמְסִלָּתוֹ)”, keeping its line.

senses.definition: Something built up for going on: what Solomon made of algum wood for the house of Yahweh and for his house.

evidence.note: “The king made of the algum wood מְסִלּוֹת for the house of Yahweh and for the king's house, and lyres and harps.”
The parallel account has מִסְעָד, a support or railing, in its place.

evidence.locator: 2Sa.20.12 (twice), 2Sa.20.13, מְסִלָּה → τρίβου; τρίβος renders מְסִלָּה ×3 in the aligned text

evidence.note: “Make his paths (τρίβους) straight”, quoting Isa 40:3, where τρίβους stands for מְסִלָּה.
“Make straight the way (ὁδόν) of the Lord”: John's own summary of Isa 40:3.

parallels.note: The way: “clear the way of Yahweh … a highway for our God”.

phrases.gloss: the highway of the Fuller's Field, at the conduit of the upper pool of Jerusalem

words.summary: A basket for bread and food: the baker's three baskets on his head, the basket of unleavened bread at the ordination of the priests and the end of a Nazirite's vow, the basket Gideon carried his offering in. The word is well attested across the Semitic languages, but how it comes from the root's sense of casting up is not clear; it may be a separate word of the same consonants.

senses.definition: A basket carried on the head or in the hand, holding bread, cakes or meat.

evidence.note: “Three baskets of white bread on my head.”
“In the uppermost basket all kinds of baked food for Pharaoh, and the birds ate them out of the basket on my head.”
The bread, cakes and wafers of the ordination “in one basket”.
The Nazirite's “basket of unleavened bread”.
Gideon “put the meat in a basket, and the broth he put in a pot”.

words.gloss: cast up, build up (a road), heap up; exalt
words.summary: Twelve times. The qal casts up earth and stones, into a road that is then cleared of stones (Isa 62:10) or into heaps and siege roads (Jer 50:26; Job 19:12); its passive participle is a road built up, the opposite of a way overgrown (Pro 15:19). The pilpel and hithpolel raise a person: to prize Wisdom highly (Pro 4:8), or to set oneself up as a bank in the way of Yahweh's people (Exo 9:17).

stems.gloss: cast up, build up (a road); heap up

senses.gloss: cast up, build up a road
senses.definition: To heap up and level a road and clear it of stones; the passive participle is a built-up road.

evidence.note: “Prepare the way of the people; סֹלּוּ סֹלּוּ הַמְסִלָּה, clear it of stones.”
“סֹלּוּ סֹלּוּ, prepare the way (פַּנּוּ־דֶרֶךְ), take up the stumbling block out of the way of my people.”
My people stumbled “from the ancient paths, to walk in byways, a way not cast up (לֹא סְלוּלָה)”.
“The way of the sluggard is as a hedge of thorns, but the path of the upright is cast up (סְלֻלָה).”

“Sing to God … סֹלּוּ for him who rides through the deserts (בָּעֲרָבוֹת)”: cast up a road for him, as Isa 40:3 “make straight in the desert (בָּעֲרָבָה) a highway”; others take it here as “lift up (a song)”.

senses.gloss: heap up; cast up (a siege road) against
senses.definition: To pile up in heaps, or to throw up a way of attack against a besieged place.

evidence.note: Of Babylon: “Open her granaries, heap her up (סָלּוּהָ) like heaps (עֲרֵמִים), and devote her to destruction.”
“His troops come together and cast up their way against me, and encamp around my tent”: the siege road.
“They cast up against me their ways of destruction.”

senses.definition: To hold in high esteem; said of Wisdom, who repays it in kind.

evidence.note: “סַלְסְלֶהָ, and she will exalt you (תְּרוֹמְמֶךָּ); she will honour you when you embrace her”: the parallel רוּם fixes the sense.

senses.definition: To raise oneself like a bank in another's way: Pharaoh's stand against Israel's going.

evidence.note: “You still מִסְתּוֹלֵל against my people, not to let them go”: the raised bank that blocks the way, set beside the refusal it explains.

words.summary: The earth cast up against a besieged city's wall, nearly always with the verb שָׁפַךְ “pour out”. Against Jerusalem it is the mark of Yahweh's judgment by Babylon (Jer 6:6; 32:24; Ezk 4:2); its absence, of his defence of the city in Hezekiah's day (2Ki 19:32).

senses.definition: A mound of earth heaped against a city wall to bring attackers level with it.

evidence.note: Against Abel Beth-maacah: “They poured out a mound against the city, and it stood against the rampart, and all the people with Joab battered the wall to throw it down.”
Of the king of Assyria: “He shall not come into this city, nor shoot an arrow there, nor come before it with shield, nor pour out a mound against it.”
“Cut down her trees and pour out a mound against Jerusalem.”
“The mounds have come to the city to take it.”
The houses torn down “against the mounds and against the sword”.
“Lay siege against it, build a siege wall (דָּיֵק) against it, pour out a mound against it, set camps against it, and battering rams.”
Against Tyre.
“The king of the north shall come and pour out a mound and take a fortified city.”

evidence.locator: Isa.37.33; Jer.33.4; Ezk.4.2; Ezk.26.8, סֹלְלָה → χάραξ

evidence.note: Jesus over Jerusalem: “Your enemies will cast a χάραξ about you and surround you”: the Septuagint's word for the סֹלְלָה of Jer 6:6 and Ezk 4:2.

phrases.gloss: pour out (throw up) a siege mound

words.summary: Once, the stairway of Jacob's dream at Bethel, set on the earth with its top reaching heaven: something built up to go up by. Jesus takes up the picture of the angels going up and down for himself (Jhn 1:51).

senses.definition: A way built up for climbing, reaching from the earth to a height.

evidence.note: “Behold, a סֻלָּם set up on the earth, and its top reached to heaven, and behold, the angels of God going up and coming down on it.”
“You shall see heaven opened, and the angels of God going up and coming down upon the Son of man”: the dream's words applied to Jesus.

senses.definition: A built-up road; once, of the way of holiness on which the redeemed return to Zion.

evidence.note: “A מַסְלוּל shall be there, and a way, and it shall be called the way of holiness; the unclean shall not pass over it.”
“The ransomed of Yahweh shall return and come to Zion with singing.”

words.summary: Once, in the plural, in the gleaning of Israel's remnant. The doubled form of סַל; the Targum's Aramaic has the grape-cutter's small baskets. Whether the gleaner's hand goes back to the baskets or over the vine's shoots, the verse does not settle; its tie to the root is as unclear as סַל's.

senses.definition: What the grape-gatherer turns his hand back to (or over) in gleaning a vine: on the Aramaic's evidence, his small baskets.

evidence.note: “They shall thoroughly glean the remnant of Israel as a vine; turn back your hand as a grape-gatherer upon the סַלְסִלּוֹת.”

cognates.note: A street or lane in Akkadian, from the first millennium on; it answers to מְסִלָּה and מַסְלוּל, the made road. The written s and š vary in the Akkadian.

evidence.locator: armep x000019070, šulû [street] N; armep x000063120, sulû [street] N

cognates.note: The same basket word, common in Middle and Neo-Assyrian and Babylonian; it bears on סַל, not on the root's casting up.

evidence.locator: armep x000030480, sallu [tray] N, meanings basket, tray

cognates.note: Jewish Aramaic: the Targum's word for the baker's baskets of Gen 40.

evidence.locator: s.v. סַלָּא I (ch.), citing Targ. Gen. XL, 16–18; pl. סַלַּיָּא, סַלִּין

cognates.note: Jewish Aramaic: the Targum's rendering of סַלְסִלּוֹת in Jer 6:9, reading the word as baskets.

evidence.locator: s.v. סַלְסִלִּין (ch.), citing Targ. Jer. VI, 9

cognates.note: Lane's sources record the word but say it was not thought to be Arabic: likely borrowed into Arabic from Aramaic, so it confirms the word but not a native Arabic root.

evidence.locator: Book I, p. 1396, art. سل, سَلَّةٌ (n20290)
evidence.note: “A [basket of the kind called] جُونَة … a receptacle in which fruit is carried … سَلَّةُ الخُبْزِ the bread-basket … سَلَّةٌ meaning as expl. above is not thought by IDrd to be an Arabic word.”

cognates.note: Jewish Aramaic, in the Targum of Jacob's dream and in the Talmud (“a round of his ladder broke”).

evidence.locator: s.v. סוּלָּמָא (ch.), citing Targ. Gen. XXVIII, 12 (printed XXVII); Y. M. Kat. I, end, 81ᵃ

cognates.gloss: ladder, series of stairs or steps
cognates.note: The same form and meaning as סֻלָּם, but Arabic files it under سلم and may have borrowed it; whether it shows a native root s-l-l is uncertain.

evidence.locator: Book I, p. 1416, art. سلم, سُلَّمٌ (n20553)
evidence.note: “A ladder, or a series of stairs or steps … upon which one ascends.”

cognates.note: Proposed as the source or cousin of the ladder word in Aramaic, Syriac and Arabic; the m and t set it apart from סֻלָּם, so the link is uncertain.

evidence.note: Lists Arabic سُلَّم, Jewish Aramaic סוּלָּמָא and Hebrew סֻלָּם among its descendants.

doctrine.statement: Isaiah calls for a road to be cast up in the desert: “Clear the way of Yahweh; make straight in the desert a highway for our God … and the glory of Yahweh shall be revealed, and all flesh shall see it together” (Isa 40:3, 5). All four Gospels say this voice was John, who prepared the way for Jesus (Mat 3:3; Mrk 1:3; Luk 3:4–6; Jhn 1:23). The same highway carries Yahweh's people home: “a highway for the remnant of his people from Assyria, as there was for Israel when he came up out of Egypt” (Isa 11:16); “a highway, and it shall be called the way of holiness … the ransomed of Yahweh shall return and come to Zion with singing” (Isa 35:8, 10); “cast up, cast up the highway … say to the daughter of Zion, behold, your salvation comes” (Isa 62:10–11); and a highway from Egypt to Assyria, when Israel is “a blessing in the midst of the earth” with them (Isa 19:23–25). From the verses: the road cast up for Yahweh was begun when John prepared for Jesus, and leads to the return of Israel's remnant to Zion and the nations' blessing with them, in the kingdom on the earth.

When Hezekiah trusted Yahweh, the word was that the king of Assyria would “not pour out a mound against” Jerusalem, “for I will defend this city to save it” (2Ki 19:32–34). When the city would not hear, Yahweh himself commanded the mound: “Cut down trees and pour out a mound against Jerusalem; this is the city to be punished” (Jer 6:6), and Jeremiah saw it done: “the mounds have come to the city to take it … what you spoke has come to pass” (Jer 32:24); Ezekiel acted it out on a brick (Ezk 4:1–2). Jesus, weeping over the city, used the Septuagint's word for the mound: “your enemies will cast a bank (χάραξ) about you … and will not leave in you one stone upon another, because you did not know the time of your visitation” (Luk 19:43–44). Rome did so in AD 70. From the verses: the siege mound against Jerusalem is Yahweh's judgment on a people who refuse his word, as Babylon's was, and its withholding his defence of those who trust him.

note: BDB's zero-token cross-references m.cr.aj, o.bi.ab and o.bm.ab are not listed. סֶלָה: BDB files it here as “lift up”; nothing in scripture or the cognates confirms that, so it is kept with an unclear tie and no kin. The Septuagint's διάψαλμα is not in the NT and is left out. סַל and סַלְסִלָּה: BDB files them in a separate section (o.bp); kept here per “one spelling, one entry”, with their own basket cognates; whether they are a second root is open. Arabic سلّ “draw out” (the brief's sound match) shares no meaning and is not recorded. Psa 68:5 סֹלּוּ is read as casting up a road (with Isa 40:3); “lift up a song” is the other reading. Exo 9:17 hithpolel: “set yourself up as a bank against” is the reading taken; check. Akkadian šulû/sulû is cited from Oracc's gloss “street”; a fuller dictionary (CAD S/Š) may confirm “raised road”. Names: TIPNR's Sallu (סַלּוּא, סַלּוּ), Sallai (סַלַּי) and Salu (סָלוּא) are not filed under this root in the brief and their root is uncertain (perhaps סלא “weigh”), so no name file was written. Jer 6:9 סַלְסִלּוֹת: basket (Targum) or vine shoots; unsettled.
